issues.issue: Section 4.2 lets the Board amend the Plan "from time to time" or terminate it "at any time" without qualification, whereas Section 10.1 permits amendment only by unanimous Board vote subject to three express conditions and Section 10.2 forbids any amendment diverting the Fund. The unconditional grant and the conditioned grant cover the same act.

The three conditions (a), (b) and (c) are run together with the trailing fragment about Section 404 deductibility appearing out of sequence, so it cannot be told which condition attaches to which return period. As written the enumerated triggers and the enumerated deadlines do not line up.

Section 4.4 authorises the Board to return contributions to an Employer, while Section 10.3(b) states that "[u]nder no circumstances shall any portion of the corpus or income of the Trust Fund, directly or indirectly, revert or accrue to the benefit of any Employer" and Section 10.2 excepts only Section 10.3. The absolute no-reversion language does not carve out Section 4.4.

The anti-alienation rule is qualified by enumerated statutory exceptions (QDROs, Section 206(d)(2) assignments) followed by the open catch-all "or as may otherwise be provided in the Plan, ERISA or the Code," leaving the reach of the general words against the specifics undefined. Because the Board writes the Plan, the exception can be read to swallow the rule.

"All reasonable and necessary expenses" is followed by a seven-item list introduced by "including, but not limited to," so whether an unlisted charge is payable from the corpus turns on the reach of the general words. The specifics give no principle for the catch-all.

Section 5.3(c) lets the Board delegate "such of its administrative duties" as it deems advisable, while Section 5.13 limits delegation to "ministerial powers or duties" and Section 5.6(a) governs delegation of fiduciary responsibilities to Committees. The three provisions set different limits on the same delegation power.

Subsection (y) authorises the Board "[g]enerally, [to] perform all acts (whether or not expressly authorized herein)" it deems necessary and prudent, a catch-all standing against twenty-four enumerated specific powers. Whether the general words are confined to the kind of acts enumerated is exactly the ejusdem generis question.

The opening words empower the Board "in its sole and absolute discretion" free of state-law limits on trust investment, while Section 5.7 subjects every exercise of power under the Agreement to a prudent-person standard and a diversification requirement. Sole and absolute discretion and a prudence duty pull against each other over the same acts.

Section 5.6(a) permits delegation of "fiduciary responsibilities" to Committees "including but not limited to" benefit applications and delinquencies, while Section 5.13 confines the Board's delegation power to "ministerial powers or duties." The scope of what may be handed off differs between the two sections.

Section 5.6(b) requires each Committee to have an equal number of Employer and Union Trustees, whereas Section 1.10 requires only "at least one Employer Trustee and one Union Trustee." A committee valid under one definition may be invalid under the other.

Section 5.7 imposes a prudent-person standard of care on every exercise of power, while Section 5.9(b) states the Trustees "shall not be personally liable for any error of judgment or for any loss arising out of any act or omission." A duty that can never be breached in damages is difficult to reconcile with the stated standard.

The clause lets Trustees treat an employer's writing as "conclusive evidence" with "no duty to make any investigation or inquiry," while Section 5.7 requires the care and diligence of a prudent person familiar with such matters. Whether a Trustee may rely without inquiry in the face of red flags is unresolved between them.

Section 5.9(a) charges the Trust Fund with "first liens" indemnifying the Trustees against "any liabilities of any kind," while Section 5.9(d) indemnifies only good-faith conduct and excludes fraud, willful misconduct and gross negligence. The two subsections of the same section set incompatible indemnity boundaries.

The blanket exculpation for "any error of judgment or... any loss arising out of any act or omission" contradicts Section 5.9(d), which expressly withholds protection for a Trustee's own fraud, willful misconduct or gross negligence, and Section 5.7's prudence standard. Read literally, subsection (b) immunises the very conduct subsection (d) carves out.

The final exclusion reads "or except as may otherwise reimbursed by insurance," omitting the verb, so it is unclear whether insurance recovery bars indemnity or merely reduces it. The gap changes who bears a loss that insurance partly covers.

Section 5.9(d) limits indemnity to good-faith acts and excludes fraud, willful misconduct and gross negligence, while Section 5.9(b) exculpates Trustees for "any act or omission" without qualification. The two provisions cannot both govern the same claim.

Section 5.12(b) allows signature authority over Fund monies to be delegated to "any two Trustees" or even to a non-Trustee, while Section 6.4(a) requires all Board action to be by unanimous vote of the two units. Whether a two-Trustee withdrawal is Board action is left unaddressed.

Section 5.13 confines delegation to "ministerial powers or duties," but Section 5.6(a) authorises delegation of fiduciary responsibilities to Committees and Section 5.5(r) authorises delegation of Plan operation duties to other persons. The instrument states two inconsistent limits on the same power.

"Complete authority, in its sole and absolute discretion, to construe the terms of the Plan or this Agreement" with decisions "final and binding upon all parties affected thereby" leaves open who counts as a party affected and what review, if any, survives. The breadth of "final and binding" is precisely the sort of term parties read differently.

The Board's self-declared final authority to construe the Agreement sits against Section 6.6, which sends questions the Board cannot decide to an AAA arbitrator, and Section 9.10, which sends employer withdrawal-liability disputes to arbitration only. Whether the Board's construction binds an Employer in those forums is unresolved.

Officer terms run "until their successors are elected," yet no provision of Article 6 or elsewhere prescribes how or when officers are elected. The instrument supplies a term of office with no election mechanism to measure it against.

Special meetings may be called "by any four Trustees," but Section 3.1 provides for only five Trustees and Amendment No. 4's replacement Section 3.1 for only four. Under the amended composition the provision requires every Trustee to join in calling a meeting, which is no minority right at all.

A quorum of two Union and two Employer Trustees is workable under the original Section 3.1 (two and three), but Amendment No. 4 reduces the Board to two and two, so the quorum requirement becomes attendance by every Trustee. Whether a quorum can still be constituted after the amendment is a genuine question across the two provisions.

The subsection first requires "unanimous vote of the Trustees" and then "unanimous vote of the two units," which are different requirements — unanimity of individuals versus unanimity of two block votes. Section 6.4(b), which lets a unit vote be cast on a bare majority, shows the two formulations cannot both be literal.

A unit vote requires "the concurring vote of a majority of all" that unit's Trustees, which cannot be produced by a two-member unit that splits, yet Amendment No. 4's Section 3.1 fixes each unit at two Trustees. The voting rule assumes an odd-numbered unit the amended composition does not provide.

"Such proxies to be valid only at the meeting immediately succeeding its execution" is ambiguous as to whether the proxy is good at the next meeting of any kind or only at the meeting for which it was given. The singular "its" against the plural "proxies" adds to the uncertainty.

Section 6.4(d) provides that a deadlocked matter "shall then be resolved by arbitration," while Section 6.6(a) makes submission depend on a Trustee's request to the Chairman. Whether arbitration is automatic or must be invoked differs between the two provisions.

"Unless otherwise specifically agreed to by both parties" presupposes two parties, but a Section 6.6 arbitration arises from a deadlock among Trustees of a single board with no defined "parties." Whose agreement can move the hearing is not answerable from the text.

The opening sentence — "Where the Administrator is a Trust Fund, subject to the terms of this Agreement..." — has no predicate, so the provision never says what the Administrator is responsible for before listing "such responsibilities." The antecedent for the enumerated duties is missing.

Item (1) gives the Board "the right to amend, modify or terminate this Agreement at any time," whereas Section 10.1 permits amendment only by unanimous vote subject to three conditions and Section 10.3(a) also allows termination by joint resolution of the Union and the Association. The unconditional grant in 7.2 cannot be squared with Article 10's machinery.
